The result does not show that synthetic respondents are inherently invalid; it shows that their apparent validity can be highly sensitive to researcher choices that need to be governed and reported.
items.attribution: Jamie Cummins — Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science
items.questionAndWhy: How much do defensible choices about model, prompts, demographics, and sampling change whether LLM-generated silicon samples appear to reproduce human data?
items.whatTheyDid: Cummins generated 252 synthetic-sample configurations in one study and 66 defensible configurations in a reanalysis, varying model, reasoning or temperature, demographic information, and sampling strategy.
items.whatTheyFound: Performance varied substantially across configurations; in one reanalysis, correlations between human and synthetic association structures ranged from .23 to .84.
items.whatItMeans: Prompting and generation settings are part of the research design. Synthetic-human work needs governed configurations and multiple validity targets because analyst choices can materially change conclusions.

items.streamTitle: AI can become “too caring to be real”
items.streamSummary: A mixed-method study found that moderate autonomy-supportive AI communication increased intimacy, conversational elaboration, and voluntary re-engagement, but highly consistent or fluent support could begin to feel scripted and reduce authenticity. Human escalation and transparent AI disclosure softened that penalty. The practical lesson is that empathic AI may need calibration rather than maximization, although the findings come from the studied AI-consumer interaction contexts and may not generalize everywhere.
items.questionAndWhy: Can supportive AI communication improve a user’s sense of connection without eventually feeling artificial?
items.whatTheyDid: Le and colleagues studied perceived autonomy support in AI communication using a staggered field rollout, a longitudinal user panel, and a between-subjects experiment.
items.whatTheyFound: Moderate autonomy-supportive communication increased intimacy, elaboration, and re-engagement, but highly consistent or fluent support could reduce authenticity; human escalation and disclosure reduced that penalty.
items.whatItMeans: More empathy-like language is not automatically better. AI relationship design may involve calibration rather than maximization.

items.streamTitle: One important behavior improved while most process measures stayed null
items.streamSummary: A 27-school cluster randomized trial found that adding R-CITY equity-focused lessons and teacher coaching to an existing social-emotional program improved one observed student outcome—physical aggression—and one teacher-reported outcome, while most other process and system measures did not significantly change. The result is valuable precisely because the nulls remain visible: a successful intervention package does not automatically reveal which component or mechanism produced the behavioral effect.
items.questionAndWhy: Can an equity-focused school intervention change observable student behavior, and do the expected process measures move with it?
items.whatTheyDid: The R-CITY trial randomized 27 schools to standard Second Step programming or Second Step plus equity-focused lessons, teacher coaching, and implementation support.
items.whatTheyFound: The added intervention improved one of six observed student-behavior outcomes—physical aggression—and one of three teacher-report outcomes—general teaching self-efficacy; most other measured outcomes were null.
items.whatItMeans: A meaningful behavioral effect can coexist with mostly null process measures. That makes it unsafe to assume a favored mediator or component caused the improvement.

items.streamTitle: More realistic agents can make a model harder to identify
items.streamSummary: A study of agent-based model calibration found that adding heterogeneous agent parameters made it harder to recover the true parameter values from model outputs. The problem is not simply computational complexity: different parameter combinations can become observationally indistinguishable when the available summary statistics are not informative enough. The result is a useful warning that richer agent descriptions do not automatically improve explanatory value; model detail has to be supported by observations that can identify it.
items.attribution: Olukan et al. — Journal of Artificial Societies and Social Simulation
items.questionAndWhy: Does adding more heterogeneous detail to an agent-based model always make it more useful or realistic?
items.whatTheyDid: Olukan and colleagues compared homogeneous and heterogeneous contagion agent-based models and used Approximate Bayesian Computation to test how accurately parameters could be recovered from simulated observations.
items.whatTheyFound: Adding heterogeneity reduced parameter-identification accuracy because multiple parameter combinations could produce similar observable outputs.
items.whatItMeans: More detail can make a model less empirically identifiable even when it looks more realistic. Modelers need observations that can actually distinguish added parameters.

items.streamTitle: Hierarchical FCMs can compress many indicators without pretending the links are causal
items.streamSummary: A hierarchical Fuzzy Cognitive Map grouped large numbers of financial indicators into a smaller set of interpretable concepts, then propagated risk across that concept layer. On two bankruptcy datasets it remained competitive with stronger nonlinear models while improving interpretability and monitoring performance. The architecture is useful for complex decision support because it separates indicator detail from higher-level reasoning, but the learned concept links are predictive or associational rather than causally identified.
items.attribution: Krimpas et al. — Journal of Risk and Financial Management
items.questionAndWhy: Can a high-dimensional predictive problem be compressed into a smaller set of interpretable concepts without giving up too much performance?
items.whatTheyDid: Krimpas and colleagues grouped correlated financial ratios into data-driven concepts and propagated risk across those concepts using a hierarchical Fuzzy Cognitive Map on two bankruptcy datasets.
items.whatTheyFound: The hierarchical FCM improved risk concentration compared with linear baselines while remaining competitive with stronger nonlinear models and preserving concept-level explanations; learned links were not presented as causally identified.
items.whatItMeans: Hierarchy can separate a noisy indicator layer from a smaller reasoning layer. An FCM-shaped model can be interpretable without its learned links becoming causal relationships.

items.streamTitle: Germany is turning hybrid-threat attribution into a broader defensive architecture
items.streamSummary: Germany is planning a wider anti-sabotage package combining mobile counter-drone units, stronger authorities for critical-infrastructure operators, a national cyber sensor network, and expanded AI-supported surveillance. The development is notable because the response is becoming a sociotechnical defense system rather than a statement of condemnation. It is still a plan, however: implementation quality, public reassurance, adversary behavior, legal sufficiency, and privacy consequences remain separate outcomes that cannot be inferred from the announcement.
items.questionAndWhy: How is Germany moving from public attribution of hybrid threats toward an integrated defensive architecture?
items.whatTheyDid: Reuters reported German Interior Ministry plans for mobile counter-drone units, expanded authorities for critical-infrastructure operators, a national cyber sensor network, and wider use of AI-supported surveillance after the Leipzig/Halle airport incident.
items.whatTheyFound: The planned response combines sensing, legal authorities, response capacity, cyber defense, and surveillance rather than relying on condemnation alone.
items.whatItMeans: This is evidence of planned defensive architecture, not proof of deterrence or effectiveness. Implementation, public reassurance, adversary adaptation, legal legitimacy, and privacy effects require separate measurement.

items.streamTitle: Influence can begin as a job, trip, or opportunity—not an argument
items.streamSummary: Taiwan’s Straits Exchange Foundation warned that youth-facing job offers, tourism, and cultural exchanges involving China can combine economic opportunity with scam, detention, data, and political-influence risks. The useful analytical point is the pathway: an initial behavioral ask can look ordinary long before any ideological or political objective becomes visible. The warning comes from a Taiwan institution engaged in cross-strait competition, so legitimate exchanges, criminal scams, political influence, and state direction should remain separate evidentiary questions.
items.attribution: Chen Yu-fu & Jonathan Chin — Taipei Times
items.questionAndWhy: How can youth-facing job, travel, and cultural-exchange offers blend ordinary opportunity with fraud risk and political influence?
items.whatTheyDid: The Taipei Times reported a Straits Exchange Foundation warning that some China-linked job offers, tours, and exchange programs aimed at Taiwanese youth may combine economic incentives with scams, data exposure, or activities Taiwan characterizes as united-front influence.
items.whatTheyFound: The warning describes an online-to-offline pathway that can begin with ordinary participation rather than explicit persuasion, while also combining several distinct risks that should not be treated as one proven state-directed mechanism.
items.whatItMeans: Influence can start with opportunity, access, and relationships rather than arguments. Scam activity, legitimate exchange, political influence, and state direction still need to be analytically separated.

items.streamTitle: A digital twin needs a continuing connection to the real world
items.streamSummary: A new architecture paper draws a useful boundary between a crowd simulation and a crowd digital twin. A true twin requires sensing and synchronization with the physical crowd and its environment, alongside prediction and decision support; representational detail alone is not enough. The framework is a roadmap rather than evidence that a fully validated crowd twin already exists, but it provides a stricter standard for claims about synthetic audiences and digital twins.
items.attribution: Casadei et al. — Future Generation Computer Systems
items.questionAndWhy: What distinguishes a true crowd digital twin from a detailed crowd simulation?
items.whatTheyDid: Casadei and colleagues synthesized crowd-management and digital-twin research into requirements, a reference architecture, and a roadmap centered on sensing, synchronization, modeling, prediction, decision support, and possible actuation.
items.whatTheyFound: A standalone simulation or detailed synthetic population is not enough to qualify as a digital twin; the architecture requires an ongoing physical-digital connection to the represented crowd and environment.
items.whatItMeans: The term digital twin should imply a data thread back to reality. Behavioral and social twins need synchronization and validation, not just richer synthetic personas.

items.streamTitle: Synthetic populations are starting to include values and ideology—not just demographics
items.streamSummary: A Bayesian population-synthesis framework adds values, ideology, opinions, and life priorities to the demographic attributes normally used to construct synthetic populations. In a Barcelona demonstration, the method reproduced important demographic and motivational distributions and dependencies across large samples. This creates a more empirical starting point for agent models than demographic personas alone, but it does not show that the resulting synthetic people will make human-like decisions or respond correctly to interventions.
items.questionAndWhy: Can synthetic populations represent values, ideology, opinions, and priorities rather than demographics alone?
items.whatTheyDid: Aguilera and colleagues built Bayesian population-synthesis models that combine demographic and motivational data and demonstrated them on Barcelona populations of up to 300,000 synthetic individuals.
items.whatTheyFound: The approach reproduced demographic and motivational distributions and dependencies, with a hybrid model balancing the two layers most effectively. The authors position this as population initialization rather than validated behavioral simulation.
items.whatItMeans: Synthetic populations can be empirically richer without becoming validated synthetic humans. Matching baseline attributes and predicting treatment response remain separate problems.

items.streamTitle: Exposure to untrustworthy sources fell about 70%; measured political attitudes did not
items.streamSummary: A multimonth randomized Meta field experiment reduced Facebook and Instagram feed exposure to repeatedly untrustworthy sources by about 70%. Despite that large change in what people saw, researchers found no measurable effects across numerous preregistered political attitudes and beliefs, including among users with high prior exposure. The result does not show that misinformation never matters. It shows why exposure is an intermediate outcome: a technically successful feed intervention can still produce a null at the attitude level.
items.questionAndWhy: If a platform sharply reduces exposure to repeatedly untrustworthy sources, do political attitudes and beliefs change?
items.whatTheyDid: Researchers working with Meta ran a multimonth randomized field experiment around the 2020 U.S. election that reduced Facebook and Instagram feed exposure to repeatedly untrustworthy sources by about 70%.
items.whatTheyFound: The intervention produced a large exposure reduction but no measurable change across numerous preregistered political attitudes and beliefs, including among users with high pretreatment exposure.
items.whatItMeans: A successful exposure intervention can produce a null downstream attitude effect. Reducing content supply is not equivalent to changing beliefs, trust, identity, or behavior.

items.streamTitle: Let an FCM learn without letting it silently invent the graph
items.streamSummary: A human-centric Fuzzy Cognitive Map framework separates reasoning over a fixed graph from a learning loop that updates weights and from explicit bounded expert correction. That architecture allows adaptation while preserving inspectable structure and a record of human intervention. It offers a useful governance pattern for decision support, but the medical benchmarks do not establish that learned edges are causal or that the method transfers unchanged to behavioral or national-security systems.
items.questionAndWhy: Can an FCM learn from data while remaining inspectable and open to bounded expert correction?
items.whatTheyDid: Zakaria proposed a medical decision-support framework with an inner FCM reasoning loop, an outer weight-learning loop constrained by an admissible topology, and an explicit expert-correction operator.
items.whatTheyFound: The approach allowed weights to adapt while preserving a governed graph structure and inspectable expert intervention. Its main advantage was transparency and editability rather than uniformly better predictive accuracy.
items.whatItMeans: Separating structure, state propagation, and parameter learning is a useful governance pattern. A learned FCM edge is still not automatically a causally identified relationship.

items.streamTitle: Ordinary citizens persuaded political opponents surprisingly often—but could not tell when they were good at it
items.streamSummary: An incentivized persuasion study asked ordinary citizens to write messages for people who disagreed with them politically. Nearly 30% of the messages shifted opinion in the intended direction and about 11% backfired. Perspective-taking and personal narratives were the strongest predictors of success, yet senders were poor judges of their own persuasive ability. The study shows meaningful message-level heterogeneity, but those features were not independently randomized, so they should not yet be treated as proven causal ingredients.
items.attribution: Naunov, Rueda-Cañón & Ryan — The Journal of Politics
items.questionAndWhy: Can ordinary citizens persuade people who disagree with them politically, and what features predict which messages work?
items.whatTheyDid: Naunov, Rueda-Cañón, and Ryan incentivized more than 400 people to write messages for political opponents, exposed opposing-view participants to those messages, and measured opinion change.
items.whatTheyFound: Nearly 30% of messages persuaded and about 11% backfired. Perspective-taking and personal narratives were the most reliable predictors of success, while senders were poor judges of their own persuasiveness.
items.whatItMeans: Persuasive ability varies substantially among ordinary communicators, and pretesting may be more useful than trusting sender confidence. The message features are predictors of success, not yet cleanly isolated causal components.

items.streamTitle: AI labels can change how people engage with the same content
items.streamSummary: Two randomized experiments found that labeling social-media content as AI-generated reduced affective and intended behavioral engagement, especially for emotional posts. Disclosure timing also mattered for some AI-enhanced content. The finding suggests that provenance labels can change the experience of a message rather than simply describe it. Because the evidence comes from immediate experimental responses, it does not establish durable changes in trust or observed behavior across an entire platform.
items.questionAndWhy: Do AI-authorship labels change how people engage with social-media content, and does the effect depend on content type or disclosure timing?
items.whatTheyDid: Seeger, Wessel, and Lehrer ran two randomized online experiments that varied whether Instagram-style content was labeled human-created, AI-enhanced, or AI-generated, along with content type and disclosure timing.
items.whatTheyFound: AI labels reduced affective and intended behavioral engagement, with the strongest penalty for emotional content. Later disclosure partly reduced the affective penalty for AI-enhanced content.
items.whatItMeans: Transparency labels are behaviorally active design elements, not neutral metadata. Immediate experimental responses do not establish durable platform behavior or long-term trust effects.

items.streamTitle: Better information reduced party-cue influence; simply thinking harder did not
items.streamSummary: Two large experiments separated access to policy information from prompts to think more effortfully. Providing substantive information reduced reliance on party cues by roughly 35% on average, while encouraging additional thought alone produced little independent effect. The result suggests that some apparent heuristic reasoning reflects an information constraint rather than simple unwillingness to deliberate. The outcomes were policy opinions, not durable political behavior, and effects varied across issues.
items.questionAndWhy: Can better policy information or simply prompting people to think harder reduce reliance on political party cues?
items.whatTheyDid: Tappin and McKay ran two large survey experiments that independently randomized party cues, access to substantive policy information, and an effortful-thinking prompt across 20 U.S. policy issues.
items.whatTheyFound: Providing policy information reduced the influence of party cues by roughly 35% on average, while prompting more effortful thinking alone produced much smaller attenuation and little evidence of an independent effect.
items.whatItMeans: Information availability and motivation to deliberate are different intervention targets. Telling people to think harder may miss the bottleneck when they lack useful information.

items.streamTitle: A government nudge changed when civil servants complied more than whether they complied
items.streamSummary: A Buenos Aires field experiment redesigned the notice attached to real freedom-of-information requests using clarity, salience, deterrence, and social-norm cues. Overall compliance did not significantly increase, but responses exactly at the final legal deadline rose by 10.7 percentage points. Government training workshops diluted the treatment contrast and the researchers also found intra-agency spillovers. The study shows how a treatment can shift the timing distribution while concurrent institutional activity becomes part of the causal story.
items.questionAndWhy: Can a behaviorally redesigned government notice improve freedom-of-information compliance, and how do concurrent training and spillovers change the observed effect?
items.whatTheyDid: Scartascini and Zamora worked with Buenos Aires to cluster-randomize redesigned FOI notices containing clarity, salience, deterrence, and social-norm elements across real requests handled by government agencies.
items.whatTheyFound: The notice did not significantly raise overall compliance but increased responses exactly at the 25-day legal deadline by 10.7 percentage points. Concurrent government workshops diluted the contrast, and the study found evidence of within-agency spillovers.
items.whatItMeans: Behavioral interventions operate inside institutions, not laboratory vacuums. Timing, contamination, training, and spillovers can be part of the causal effect rather than mere implementation noise.

items.streamTitle: Causal discovery can help explain an LLM simulation before it explains society
items.streamSummary: CAMO is a new framework for tracing macro-level outcomes in LLM-agent simulations back to smaller sets of simulated mechanisms. It extracts factors from simulation records, learns compact explanatory graphs, and uses simulator-internal counterfactuals to probe ambiguous relationships. That is useful for auditing complex agent systems and identifying model-internal levers. The critical boundary is external validity: a causal pathway recovered inside a simulator is evidence about how that simulator works, not proof that humans follow the same pathway.
items.attribution: Yu et al. — Findings of ACL 2026
items.questionAndWhy: Can causal discovery make emergent outcomes inside LLM-agent simulations easier to explain and audit?
items.whatTheyDid: Yu and colleagues introduced CAMO, which converts mechanistic hypotheses and simulation logs into computable factors, learns a compact explanatory graph around an emergent target, and uses simulator counterfactuals to orient or revise uncertain edges.
items.whatTheyFound: Across four simulation settings, CAMO produced Markov boundaries, upstream explanatory subgraphs, and candidate intervention levers intended to explain which simulated mechanisms generated macro-level outcomes.
items.whatItMeans: This can help debug a simulator, but causal structure discovered inside the model is evidence about the model—not automatically about human society. External validation remains necessary.

items.streamTitle: Pacific leaders’ missile-test response shows why reassurance is part of strategic signaling
items.streamSummary: Pacific Islands Forum leaders expressed concern over China’s ICBM test and called for greater transparency and at least 24 hours’ advance notification, while Nauru dissented and Beijing rejected the criticism. The episode shows that a military demonstration communicates more than capability: warning, consultation, predictability, and perceived respect shape how regional audiences interpret it. Public concern is observable, but the episode does not yet establish a durable change in alignment, deterrence, or security behavior.
items.questionAndWhy: How did Pacific leaders interpret China’s missile test, and what does their response show about reassurance and advance notification as strategic variables?
items.whatTheyDid: Reuters reported Pacific Islands Forum leaders’ concern that China’s ICBM test crossed near several island nations without adequate warning and their call for greater transparency and at least 24 hours’ advance notice; Nauru dissented.
items.whatTheyFound: Regional concern focused not only on the military capability but also on predictability, consultation, transparency, and respect for regional actors, while Beijing rejected the criticism.
items.whatItMeans: Strategic signaling is interpreted through relationships and reassurance as well as raw capability. A military demonstration can produce different effects depending on whether recipients feel informed, respected, threatened, or ignored.

items.streamTitle: Movement and environmental feedback can reverse cooperation dynamics
items.streamSummary: A mathematical public-goods model shows how spatial movement can reverse seemingly intuitive cooperation dynamics. Under some conditions, diffusion increased cooperation and public-good availability, while strong movement of cooperators toward resource-rich areas reduced both cooperation and environmental quality. The result is theoretical rather than a human behavioral estimate, but it illustrates an important systems lesson: changing where people cluster, connect, or move can alter the incentives and feedback that determine collective outcomes.
items.attribution: Zhao et al. — Bulletin of Mathematical Biology
items.questionAndWhy: Can movement and environmental feedback change or even reverse cooperation dynamics in a spatial public-goods system?
items.whatTheyDid: Zhao and colleagues developed a reaction–diffusion–taxis model in which cooperators, defectors, and a produced public good evolve across space, then analyzed stability and simulated movement toward resource-rich regions.
items.whatTheyFound: Diffusion-driven instability could increase cooperation and public-good availability, while strong directed movement of cooperators toward higher public-good concentrations could reduce cooperation and environmental quality.
items.whatItMeans: Individually sensible movement can create worse collective outcomes through spatial feedback. The result is theoretical and requires empirical calibration before being applied to human populations.

items.streamTitle: Rich LLM digital twins still predicted individual human behavior weakly
items.streamSummary: A Science Advances mega-study built individualized LLM digital twins from more than 500 prior answers per person and tested them across 19 preregistered studies, 164 outcomes, and 1,784 participants. Average twin–human prediction correlations were only about .20, with systematic problems including stereotyping, ideological bias, hyper-rationality, and overly compressed responses. The study tests current approaches rather than placing a ceiling on future systems, but it is strong evidence that rich personal context and fluent personas do not automatically produce reliable individual behavioral prediction.
items.questionAndWhy: Can richly personalized LLM digital twins predict new choices made by the same real people?
items.whatTheyDid: Peng and colleagues ran 19 preregistered studies spanning 164 outcomes and 1,784 people, building a digital twin for each participant from more than 500 prior answers.
items.whatTheyFound: Twin predictions correlated only weakly with the corresponding human responses on average, around r=.20, and showed systematic distortions including stereotyping, representation bias, ideological bias, hyper-rationality, and compressed response distributions.
items.whatItMeans: Detailed personas and extensive personal histories do not guarantee individual behavioral fidelity. Synthetic-human systems need direct held-out behavioral benchmarks rather than face validity.

items.streamTitle: Saying “you” can trigger reactance and persuade less than saying “I”
items.streamSummary: Across seven experiments, recommendations framed as “you’ll like this” were often less persuasive than first-person statements such as “I like this.” Second-person wording increased psychological reactance, particularly among people already prone to reactance and when the recommender had little reason to know the audience’s preferences. The effect largely disappeared for close friends. The finding suggests that personalization without legitimate audience knowledge can feel controlling rather than relevant, although most outcomes were evaluations or intentions rather than durable real-world behavior.
items.questionAndWhy: Is second-person recommendation language more persuasive than first-person language, or can directly telling people what they will like trigger reactance?
items.whatTheyDid: Yin and colleagues ran seven experiments comparing first-person recommendations such as “I like this” with second-person framing such as “you’ll like this,” including tests of reactance and source knowledge.
items.whatTheyFound: Audiences were generally more persuaded by first-person framing; second-person language increased reactance, especially among high-reactance people and when the source lacked genuine knowledge of the audience. The penalty largely disappeared for close friends.
items.whatItMeans: Language intended to feel personalized can instead feel presumptuous or autonomy-threatening. Personalization works differently when the source has legitimate knowledge of the recipient.

items.streamTitle: Norms tighten when observers are present—and more when they have higher status
items.streamSummary: A cross-cultural study of 25,384 adults in 90 societies found that everyday behaviors were judged more constrained when other people were present and more constrained still when observers held higher status. The pattern suggests that norms are not simply fixed rules attached to a behavior or culture; audience presence and hierarchy change the social constraint around the same act. The outcomes were appropriateness judgments rather than observed behavior, so the study is strongest as evidence about normative perception.
items.attribution: Simpson et al. — American Sociological Review
items.questionAndWhy: Do social norms become more restrictive when other people are present, and does observer status matter?
items.whatTheyDid: Simpson and an international collaboration collected normative judgments from 25,384 adults across 90 societies for everyday behaviors performed alone, before peers, or before higher-status observers.
items.whatTheyFound: Nearly all behaviors were judged more constrained when others were present and more constrained still before higher-status observers; the observer effect varied across cultures while the added status effect was comparatively stable.
items.whatItMeans: Normative constraint is relational rather than a fixed property of a behavior. Observability and status can change how the same preference or behavior is expressed.

items.streamTitle: AI assistance increased real property-tax appeal filing—but benefits were unequal
items.streamSummary: A preregistered field experiment with 645 Dallas County households found that adding an AI chatbot to an otherwise similar personalized tax-appeal website increased self-filed appeals from 41.4% to 50.5%. Most households with access used the assistant, and process data suggest it helped people work through available information. The effect was smaller among less-advantaged households, showing that equal access to an AI tool does not guarantee equal behavioral benefit. The study is an NBER working paper and the longer-run financial outcomes remain separate questions.
items.attribution: Holz et al. — NBER Working Paper
items.questionAndWhy: Can an AI assistant reduce decision friction enough to change a consequential administrative behavior, and do benefits differ across households?
items.whatTheyDid: A preregistered field experiment with 645 Dallas County households randomized access to a tax-appeal website with or without an AI chatbot while holding the underlying personalized information and evidence constant.
items.whatTheyFound: AI access increased self-filed property-tax appeals from 41.4% to 50.5%, with 78% of treated households starting a chatbot conversation. The increase was smaller among less-advantaged households.
items.whatItMeans: AI assistance can change real behavior, but equal access does not imply equal benefit. Process and subgroup outcomes matter alongside the average treatment effect.

items.streamTitle: An intervention can keep propagating through social networks after researchers leave
items.streamSummary: A field experiment in 16 Ugandan villages randomly assigned about 40% of households to a perspective-taking conversation about refugees. Treated participants showed warmer attitudes immediately, but the influence process did not stop there: two to three weeks later, untreated people with more treated network neighbors also tended to hold warmer views, especially through strong ties. The endpoint was attitude rather than observed behavior, but the study provides unusually useful evidence that interpersonal spillovers can continue after formal exposure ends.
items.questionAndWhy: Can the effects of a persuasion intervention continue spreading through social networks after direct treatment ends?
items.whatTheyDid: Larson and Lewis mapped social networks in 16 Ugandan villages and randomly assigned roughly 40% of households to a perspective-taking conversation about refugees, then measured attitudes immediately and weeks later.
items.whatTheyFound: Treated participants became warmer immediately, and later attitudes also changed among untreated people with greater exposure to treated network neighbors, especially through strong ties.
items.whatItMeans: The treated person can become part of the intervention for others. Evaluations that assume independent units can miss important spillover and persistence.

items.streamTitle: Propaganda was more persuasive when appeals matched stable psychological needs
items.streamSummary: A multi-method study in China found that propaganda appeals tied to belonging, self-esteem, or value expression produced larger pro-regime attitude shifts among people whose corresponding psychological need was stronger. A follow-up that primed the need without matching the content did not produce the same pattern, supporting a message–audience fit interpretation rather than simple activation. The results strengthen the case for heterogeneous persuasion effects, though the outcomes were mainly attitudes and the political context limits simple generalization.
items.questionAndWhy: Why does political propaganda resonate more with some people than others, and does message–need fit explain heterogeneous effects?
items.whatTheyDid: Shen combined three rounds of survey experiments in China, a seven-day mobile-news lab-in-the-field, state-media text analysis, and field interviews to test appeals tied to belonging, self-esteem, and value expression.
items.whatTheyFound: Matched appeals produced larger pro-regime attitude shifts among people whose corresponding psychological need was stronger, while merely priming needs without matching the propaganda content did not reproduce the same pattern.
items.whatItMeans: Audience segmentation is more informative when it predicts differential treatment response. Stable psychological orientations can moderate persuasion, but the evidence is primarily attitudinal and context-specific.

items.streamTitle: A social-media virtual twin needs networks, recommenders, and feedback loops—not just personas
items.streamSummary: YSocial is a modular LLM-powered virtual social-media environment in which agents can post, comment, react, follow, receive recommendations, and reshape their network over time. A demonstration used two 500-agent partisan populations across 60 simulated days, making exposure and topology part of the model rather than treating each persona as an isolated respondent. The architecture is useful for studying platform feedback, but the authors appropriately describe it as a virtual rather than validated digital twin because real-world behavioral calibration remains limited.
items.attribution: Rossetti et al. — Big Data & Society
items.questionAndWhy: What does a social-media simulation need beyond isolated LLM personas to represent platform-level dynamics?
items.whatTheyDid: Rossetti and colleagues introduced YSocial, a modular virtual social-media environment with posting, commenting, reactions, following, recommendation, temporal activity, evolving networks, and human-agent interaction.
items.whatTheyFound: A demonstration with two 500-agent partisan populations ran for 60 simulated days and allowed recommender systems and agent choices to reshape network topology and exposure. The authors explicitly stop short of claiming a validated real-world digital twin.
items.whatItMeans: A synthetic audience becomes more realistic architecturally when content, networks, recommenders, and repeated behavior co-evolve, but richer architecture does not by itself establish human predictive validity.

items.streamTitle: Participatory FCMs can expose local leverage assumptions without pretending they are causal estimates
items.streamSummary: A participatory Fuzzy Cognitive Mapping study in Oaxaca combined ten local facilitators’ mental models into a 27-component, 43-edge consensus map and used it to compare shallow and deeper leverage points for agroecological adoption. The value is methodological: local knowledge defines an inspectable hypothesis space, while scenario analysis makes it decision-relevant. The authors explicitly caution that the edge weights are subjective judgments and the simulated leverage points are hypotheses, not experimentally identified causal effects.
items.attribution: Garcia et al. — People and Nature
items.questionAndWhy: Can participatory Fuzzy Cognitive Maps turn local expert knowledge into inspectable leverage-point scenarios without pretending the resulting weights are empirical causal estimates?
items.whatTheyDid: Garcia and colleagues combined individual mental models from 10 agroecological facilitators into a 27-component, 43-edge consensus FCM and organized candidate interventions across leverage-point depths.
items.whatTheyFound: Scenario analysis suggested combining near-term barriers such as cost and risk with deeper enabling conditions such as market access, capacity building, inclusion, and long-term vision. The authors explicitly describe the map as subjective stakeholder knowledge rather than formal causal identification.
items.whatItMeans: Participatory FCMs can make local assumptions, disagreements, and candidate leverage points explicit before false precision is imposed. Provenance matters as much as the modeled scenario output.

items.streamTitle: Seeing fewer competitors can make people compete more
items.streamSummary: An incentivized experiment found that aggregate information about peers’ competition choices could produce counter-conformity rather than imitation. When participants saw that relatively few peers had entered a tournament, they became more likely to enter themselves, consistent with interpreting low participation as a strategic opportunity rather than a norm to follow. The study uses a selected sample of competitive MBA students, so the exact effect should not be generalized broadly, but it shows why “social information” does not imply one universal mechanism.
items.questionAndWhy: Does information about what peers are doing always produce conformity, or can people interpret it strategically and move in the opposite direction?
items.whatTheyDid: An incentivized experiment with MBA students in India varied whether participants saw aggregate peer tournament-entry rates, one random person’s choice, or control information before making a second competition decision.
items.whatTheyFound: Aggregate peer information changed later tournament entry while the random-person condition did not. When observed competition was low—especially below roughly 40%—participants became more likely to enter rather than conform to the low rate.
items.whatItMeans: Social information can signal opportunity or opponent strength, not just social proof. The same descriptive norm can push behavior in opposite directions depending on the strategic setting.

items.streamTitle: German grid incidents show why the hybrid-threat narrative should not outrun attribution evidence
items.streamSummary: German authorities investigated suspected electricity-grid sabotage while a handwritten letter claimed responsibility, but officials had not established that the writer caused the incidents or publicly tied the cases to Russia. The story unfolded amid heightened concern about hybrid threats and a nearby election. That makes the case analytically useful: physical disruption, attribution confidence, elite framing, public threat perception, and electoral effects are separate questions. A broader security narrative should not be used as proof of who conducted a specific incident.
items.questionAndWhy: How should analysts separate physical sabotage, claims of responsibility, broader hybrid-threat framing, and any downstream influence effect when attribution remains unresolved?
items.whatTheyDid: Reuters reported German investigations into suspected electricity-grid sabotage, a handwritten claim of responsibility, and official concern amid a broader hybrid-threat context.
items.whatTheyFound: Authorities had not established the perpetrator of the latest grid incidents or linked them publicly to Russia, despite separate recent German attribution of the Leipzig drone incident.
items.whatItMeans: Incidents can create informational effects before attribution is settled, but analysts should not let the broader hybrid-threat narrative substitute for evidence about sponsor, motive, or audience effect.

items.streamTitle: Collective victimization does not mechanically produce revenge
items.streamSummary: A Nature Reviews Psychology synthesis argues that collective victimization can lead to very different outcomes because groups differ in how they interpret harm, assess control and resources, and cope with it. The framework separates the victimization event from beliefs, appraisal, perceived agency, coping strategy, and later behavior. Its value is conceptual rather than a single new causal estimate: grievance should not be treated as a fixed-sign predictor of hostility when solidarity, meaning-making, or constructive action are also possible.
items.attribution: Vollhardt et al. — Nature Reviews Psychology
items.questionAndWhy: Why does collective victimization lead some groups toward revenge but others toward solidarity or constructive action?
items.whatTheyDid: Vollhardt and colleagues synthesized social, clinical, community, and liberation psychology into an appraisal–coping framework for collective-victimization beliefs.
items.whatTheyFound: The review separates primary meaning appraisal, perceived resources and control, coping strategies, and downstream outcomes, showing multiple possible pathways from group harm.
items.whatItMeans: Collective harm should not be modeled as a single fixed-sign cause of hostility. Interpretation, agency, coping options, and context determine which pathway becomes likely.

items.streamTitle: Nudges and boosts both reduced electricity use—but the expected mechanism advantage did not appear
items.streamSummary: A 24-week randomized field experiment found that both normative feedback and competence-building energy tips reduced real household electricity use relative to control. Contrary to the preregistered prediction, the “boost” did not outperform the nudge, competence gains were limited, engagement with tips declined, and effects weakened late in the trial. The study is valuable because it separates a behavioral treatment effect from the theory about why one method should have been superior.
items.questionAndWhy: Do nudges and competence-building boosts differ in their ability to reduce real electricity use over time?
items.whatTheyDid: Paunov and colleagues randomized 140 student households to control, weekly social-comparison feedback, or device-specific energy-saving guidance and tracked 6,177 weekly measurements over 24 weeks.
items.whatTheyFound: Both interventions reduced electricity use, but the boost did not outperform the nudge as hypothesized; competence gains were weak and engagement declined over time.
items.whatItMeans: A treatment can change behavior while the expected mechanism advantage fails. Longer field trials also expose fatigue and decay.

items.streamTitle: Persona-prompted LLMs predicted individual behavior only modestly—and a simple classifier did better
items.streamSummary: A Scientific Reports benchmark tested LLM personas against actual social-media reactions from 1,511 people. Although headline accuracy looked respectable, class-sensitive metrics showed only modest individual prediction, and a conventional TF-IDF classifier performed better on the key like/dislike task. The study is valuable because it asks whether agents predict specific people’s behavior rather than whether their prose sounds human. It suggests that narrative-testing systems need strong behavioral baselines and should not equate persona plausibility with treatment-response fidelity.
items.questionAndWhy: How well do persona-prompted LLM agents predict specific people’s actual social-media reactions?
items.whatTheyDid: Bojić and colleagues benchmarked more than 120,000 agent–persona combinations derived from 1,511 Serbian participants across 27 LLMs and compared predictions with real like/dislike/comment/share/no-reaction labels.
items.whatTheyFound: LLM agents showed genuine but modest predictive signal; a simple TF-IDF supervised classifier outperformed them on the key binary metric.
items.whatItMeans: Believable persona output is not the same as individual response prediction. Human-simulation systems need class-sensitive benchmarks against simple non-LLM baselines.

items.streamTitle: Polarization research is heavily U.S.-weighted, making global transfer risky
items.streamSummary: A broad Nature Communications review finds that political-polarization research remains disproportionately shaped by the United States: 43% of country-referencing papers in its bibliometric set mentioned the U.S., with additional U.S.-focused work hidden among studies that did not name a country. The authors show that ideological, affective, institutional, economic, media, and platform pathways differ across political systems. The implication is straightforward: exporting a U.S.-derived polarization model or intervention abroad can import the wrong assumptions.
items.questionAndWhy: How portable is the political-polarization evidence base across countries and political systems?
items.whatTheyDid: Falkenberg and an interdisciplinary team reviewed 2,243 country-referencing polarization papers and synthesized pathways across institutions, economics, media, social media, and AI.
items.whatTheyFound: More than 43% of papers mentioning a country referenced the United States, and the review found substantial cross-system variation in mechanisms and constructs.
items.whatItMeans: U.S.-derived measures, priors, and interventions should not be assumed to transfer globally. Context and transportability need explicit treatment.

items.streamTitle: Fifteen democracies reveal six different ways to organize counter-disinformation
items.streamSummary: A comparative governance analysis of 15 democracies identifies six recurring ways governments organize counter-disinformation work, ranging from distributed coordination to dedicated agencies, embedded security functions, public-private partnerships, and societal approaches. The countries differed in centralization, specialization, legal obligations, enforcement, and resilience framing. The study does not experimentally compare effectiveness, but it shifts attention from individual tools to the national response architecture that determines who senses, attributes, coordinates, and acts.
items.questionAndWhy: How do democracies organize national counter-disinformation capabilities, and is there one dominant institutional model?
items.whatTheyDid: Tagarev compared 15 democracies across government, security, civil society, media, academia, and private actors, developing actor/task taxonomies and six institutional models.
items.whatTheyFound: The countries varied across centralization, specialization, non-state obligations, enforcement orientation, and security-versus-resilience framing; no single architecture dominated.
items.whatItMeans: Counter-disinformation capability is a response ecosystem. Organizational design can shape sensing, coordination, legitimacy, and timeliness even when countries use similar tools.

items.streamTitle: Facebook corrections changed comments and reactions—but not sharing
items.streamSummary: A randomized naturalistic Facebook intervention had trained health-care volunteers post corrective replies to COVID-19 vaccine discussions. The corrections reduced comments and some affective reactions, particularly on newer and anti-vaccine posts, but researchers found little evidence that sharing declined. The result shows why “engagement” should not be treated as one outcome: interaction, affective response, and diffusion can move differently, and none of them automatically demonstrates belief change or lower misinformation prevalence.
items.questionAndWhy: How does a volunteer-led social correction on Facebook change different forms of user behavior?
items.whatTheyDid: Cornelson and colleagues used randomized variation in post ordering and whether trained health-worker replies were actually posted to vaccine discussions.
items.whatTheyFound: Corrections reduced comments and some affective reactions, especially on newer and anti-vaccine posts, but produced little evidence of reduced sharing.
items.whatItMeans: Comments, reactions, and shares are distinct behavioral outcomes. “Engagement” is too coarse to stand in for belief, diffusion, or total misinformation prevalence.

items.streamTitle: Broadening the definition of “us” reduced discriminatory attitudes and behavior
items.streamSummary: A large randomized field intervention involving 8,648 young people in India tested an educational program designed to strengthen identification with all humanity rather than one specific outgroup. The program reduced discriminatory attitudes and behaviors across social divides and improved broader prosocial and civic outcomes. The result is notable because it targets the scope of identity itself, though the precise mediating pathway and transfer to other countries, age groups, or conflict settings require additional evidence.
items.attribution: Farid et al. — Nature Human Behaviour
items.questionAndWhy: Can expanding people’s sense of shared human identity reduce discriminatory attitudes and behavior across group divides?
items.whatTheyDid: Farid and colleagues tested an intensive educational intervention grounded in Identification With All Humanity among 8,648 young people in India.
items.whatTheyFound: The randomized field intervention reduced discriminatory attitudes and behaviors and increased broader prosocial and civic outcomes.
items.whatItMeans: Identity scope can be modified and may affect multiple intergroup outcomes. The large field trial supports the intervention in its context, while transfer and exact mediation still need separate evidence.

items.streamTitle: Persona prompting is not enough for social simulation
items.streamSummary: A peer-reviewed framework organizes LLM social simulation into six architectural levels, from static prompts to systems with persistent state, environmental coupling, multi-agent coordination, and adaptive institutions. Its central point is useful: a mechanism that depends on memory, repeated interaction, reputation, or feedback cannot be represented faithfully by a one-shot persona prompt, no matter how capable the underlying model is. The continuum is a design framework rather than an empirical law, but it clarifies what needs to be validated.
items.attribution: Haase & Pokutta — Humanities and Social Sciences Communications
items.questionAndWhy: What architecture does an LLM social simulation need to represent increasingly complex social mechanisms?
items.whatTheyDid: Haase and Pokutta proposed a six-level continuum from static LLM use through persistent state, goals, environmental coupling, multi-agent coordination, and adaptive institutions.
items.whatTheyFound: The framework maps architectural capabilities to the kinds of mechanisms a simulation can plausibly instantiate and the validity targets appropriate at each level.
items.whatItMeans: A stronger language model cannot compensate for an architecture that omits memory, interaction, feedback, or adaptation required by the claimed mechanism.

items.streamTitle: Most fuzzy “causal” models in one systematic review were predictive, not formal causal inference
items.streamSummary: A PRISMA review of 37 fuzzy-modeling studies found that only two explicitly implemented formal causal-inference frameworks. Most used predictive or associative modeling while their directed structures invited causal interpretation, and overall risk of bias was moderate to high. The reviewed domain was health care, but the methodological warning is broader: a signed arrow or Fuzzy Cognitive Map can make a causal theory executable without establishing that its edges are identified causal effects.
items.questionAndWhy: How often do fuzzy models labeled or interpreted as causal actually implement formal causal-inference methods?
items.whatTheyDid: A PRISMA systematic review examined 37 health-care studies using fuzzy inference systems, Fuzzy Cognitive Maps, and neuro-fuzzy approaches.
items.whatTheyFound: Only two explicitly implemented formal causal-inference frameworks; most were predictive or associative while carrying implicit causal interpretations, and overall risk of bias was moderate to high.
items.whatItMeans: A directed fuzzy graph can represent a causal theory without identifying causal effects. Edge provenance and epistemic status need to remain explicit.

items.streamTitle: Causal discovery can model events with duration and overlap
items.streamSummary: Niagara extends causal discovery from point events to interval events that persist and overlap. That matters for settings where a campaign, grievance, sanction, crisis, or narrative remains active while another exposure occurs. The peer-reviewed method can represent causal mechanisms that depend on concurrent states and includes identifiability results under its assumptions. Like other observational causal-discovery methods, it remains assumption-dependent, but it highlights why timing needs more than a timestamp.
items.questionAndWhy: Can causal discovery represent events that persist and overlap rather than treating everything as instantaneous points?
items.whatTheyDid: Cornanguer, Cüppers, and Vreeken introduced Niagara, a causal model and discovery algorithm for interval-based event sequences, with minimum-description-length selection and validation on synthetic and real data.
items.whatTheyFound: Niagara can represent causal mechanisms that depend on event duration and whether other events are active concurrently, with identifiability guarantees under its assumptions.
items.whatItMeans: Many real influence and social processes have onset, duration, overlap, and recovery. Temporal causal models can capture context that static or point-event representations miss.

items.streamTitle: Repeated operations can communicate jurisdiction without a traditional message
items.streamSummary: China’s seabed survey and coast-guard patrols east of Taiwan paired physical presence with administrative language describing the activity as routine law enforcement and territorial management, while Taiwan rejected Beijing’s jurisdiction and framed the activity as harassment. The case illustrates how operations, maps, legal terminology, and repetition can jointly communicate normality and control. The activities and statements are observable; the intended influence strategy and any resulting audience effects are still analytical inferences.
items.questionAndWhy: How can repeated physical operations and administrative language jointly communicate jurisdiction in a contested area?
items.whatTheyDid: Reuters reported a PRC seabed survey and repeated coast-guard patrols east of Taiwan, alongside Beijing’s language of routine law enforcement and territorial planning and Taiwan’s rejection of those claims.
items.whatTheyFound: The episode combines physical presence, repetition, bureaucratic labeling, mapping, and competing sovereignty narratives.
items.whatItMeans: Strategic communication can be embedded in actions and administrative routines, not only messages. The audience effect and inferred strategic intent remain unproven.

items.streamTitle: A correction weakens the claim that GPT-4’s persuasion advantage came from personalization
items.streamSummary: A formal correction to a widely discussed GPT-4 persuasion study narrows what the evidence supports. Personalized Human–AI conversations still outperformed the Human–Human baseline, but the direct comparison between personalized and non-personalized GPT-4 conversations did not reach statistical significance. The broader persuasion result remains; what changes is the mechanistic claim. The correction is a useful reminder that a successful system does not prove which component caused the advantage.
items.questionAndWhy: Did GPT-4’s persuasion advantage come specifically from personalization, or from the system’s broader conversational capability?
items.whatTheyDid: Nature Human Behaviour issued an Author Correction narrowing the interpretation of a 2025 persuasion experiment after the direct personalized-versus-nonpersonalized AI contrast was recognized as nonsignificant at P=.07.
items.whatTheyFound: The broader Human–AI persuasion advantage remained, but the evidence no longer supports confidently attributing that advantage specifically to personalization.
items.whatItMeans: A system-level effect is not automatically a component-level effect. Direct incremental contrasts are needed before crediting personalization or targeting.

items.streamTitle: Hybrid recruitment can move from online contact to real-world microtasks
items.streamSummary: Denmark’s security service warned that Russian intelligence is using social-media and gaming platforms to recruit people for low-friction tasks such as photographing defense firms or infrastructure that could support sabotage planning. The behavioral pathway is notable because participants may comply for money, curiosity, grievance, or convenience without adopting the sponsor’s ideology—or even fully understanding who is behind the request. The public evidence supports the warning and described pattern, while specific attributed operations remain intelligence claims disputed by Russia.
items.questionAndWhy: How are Danish authorities describing online recruitment for sabotage-enabling tasks, and what does the pathway look like from digital contact to physical action?
items.whatTheyDid: Reuters reported a PET warning that Russian services had attempted to recruit Danes through social media and gaming platforms for tasks such as photographing firms or infrastructure.
items.whatTheyFound: The warning describes a ladder from online contact to low-friction microtasks that can support intelligence collection or sabotage, while Russia disputes the allegations.
items.whatItMeans: Hybrid operations can recruit behavior without requiring ideological conversion. Contact, compliance, escalation, and operational effect should be measured separately.

items.streamTitle: Shared identity made political role models more relatable—but did not increase engagement
items.streamSummary: A multi-method study found that shared identities—especially partisanship and, for some respondents, race—made women political role models feel more relatable and inspiring. But those proximal changes did not translate into greater political interest, efficacy, or ambition. The finding is a useful caution for audience–messenger matching: similarity can improve identification without producing the downstream behavior or engagement planners actually care about.
items.questionAndWhy: Does sharing identity with a political role model make the role model more relatable—and does that translate into greater political engagement?
items.whatTheyDid: Nielsen combined a conjoint experiment, an animated-story survey experiment, and observational analysis to test shared partisanship and race in women political role models.
items.whatTheyFound: Shared identities increased relatability and inspiration, but the treatment did not increase political interest, efficacy, or nascent ambition.
items.whatItMeans: Audience–messenger similarity can move a proximal perception without moving the downstream target. Relatability should not be treated as an influence effect by itself.

items.streamTitle: Door-to-door canvassing increased registration—but most assigned households never received the full treatment
items.streamSummary: A field experiment used door-to-door canvassing to recruit residents for the Southampton Citizens’ Climate Assembly. Canvassing increased actual registration, but the implementation funnel was steep: only about two-thirds of assigned addresses received a knock attempt, 38% had any contact, and 24% received the full treatment script. The study makes a critical evaluation point visible: an intervention can lose most of its potential effect before the message is actually delivered, so implementation failure should not be confused with audience resistance.
items.attribution: Tabero et al. — European Journal of Political Research
items.questionAndWhy: Can door-to-door canvassing increase actual registration for a high-commitment citizens’ assembly, and where does the intervention lose people?
items.whatTheyDid: A block-randomized field experiment assigned 1,224 Southampton addresses to canvassing and tracked attempts, contacts, full scripts, and actual registration.
items.whatTheyFound: Canvassing increased registration, but only 64.9% received a knock attempt, 37.7% had contact, and 23.9% received the full script; opportunity cost and availability dominated stated barriers.
items.whatItMeans: Implementation can fail before a behavioral mechanism is engaged. Assignment, attempted contact, exposure, comprehension, intention, and completed behavior should remain separate.

items.streamTitle: Synthetic students need to match both baseline behavior and response to intervention
items.streamSummary: Microsoft’s StudentSim trains individualized LLM “students” from pooled data and sparse personal records, then evaluates two different targets: whether the simulator resembles the learner’s usual responses and whether it changes appropriately when given guidance. It outperformed a general frontier model across chess, writing, and mathematics, and improved a proof-of-concept tutor. The key methodological lesson is that baseline resemblance is not enough—simulation is more useful when intervention responsiveness is validated separately.
items.questionAndWhy: Can an individualized LLM student simulator match a specific learner’s baseline behavior and also respond realistically to tutoring?
items.whatTheyDid: Microsoft researchers built StudentSim from pooled learner data plus sparse individual records and evaluated 60 students across chess, English writing, and mathematics.
items.whatTheyFound: StudentSim outperformed a general frontier model on both baseline behavioral fidelity and responsiveness to guidance, and a tutor trained with it performed better in a proof-of-concept chess evaluation.
items.whatItMeans: Human simulation should distinguish matching baseline behavior from matching treatment response. The preprint is promising but does not make synthetic learners substitutes for real ones.

items.streamTitle: A nationwide RCT cut electricity modestly—but only some households responded
items.streamSummary: A six-month randomized trial of 62,750 Saudi households found that peer-comparison messages combined with energy-saving tips reduced monthly electricity use by roughly 1–2%. The effect was concentrated among moderate-consumption households, with little measurable change at the lowest and highest consumption levels. Because the outcome came from smart meters, this is real behavioral evidence rather than intention. It also shows why a small average effect can conceal major differences in who has the opportunity or capacity to respond.
items.attribution: Darandary — International Review of Economics & Finance
items.questionAndWhy: Can low-cost behavioral SMS messages reduce actual household electricity use, and who responds most?
items.whatTheyDid: A six-month randomized field trial assigned 62,750 Saudi households to four SMS interventions or control and measured smart-meter electricity consumption.
items.whatTheyFound: Peer comparison plus energy-saving tips reduced monthly use by roughly 1–2%, with effects concentrated among moderate-consumption households and little change at the low and high ends.
items.whatItMeans: Average treatment effects can hide sharp differences in opportunity or ability to respond. Real behavior, exposure, and baseline state need to be measured together.

items.streamTitle: A low polarization score can hide very different audience states
items.streamSummary: Across three nationally representative U.S. surveys, researchers found that people with similarly low affective-polarization scores could be politically very different: some were relatively lukewarm toward both parties, while others were cold toward both. Those groups differed in trust, participation, democratic attitudes, and demographics. The study is descriptive rather than causal, but it shows how a convenient difference score can erase meaningful structure that matters for audience segmentation.
items.questionAndWhy: Can a low affective-polarization score conceal fundamentally different political attitudes?
items.whatTheyDid: Versteegen, Phillips, and Mason analyzed three nationally representative U.S. surveys and decomposed the common relative-affect polarization score into underlying party-affect profiles.
items.whatTheyFound: People classified as similarly unpolarized separated into groups that were lukewarm toward both parties versus cold toward both, with different trust, participation, and democratic attitudes.
items.whatItMeans: Summary indices can collapse substantively different states. Preserve underlying components when they may imply different behaviors or interventions.

items.streamTitle: Do not invent your agents’ belief structure when empirical data can seed it
items.streamSummary: SimPol builds belief networks from survey data across 23 European countries and uses those empirically inferred structures to initialize an agent-based polarization model. The simulated dynamics then vary with parameters such as belief rigidity and susceptibility to social influence. The architecture is valuable because it separates empirical baseline structure from theory-driven update rules instead of inventing synthetic agents from scratch. It remains a preprint, and matching broad patterns is not the same as demonstrating causal or predictive validity.
items.questionAndWhy: Can agent-based polarization simulations be initialized from empirically inferred belief networks rather than invented belief structures?
items.whatTheyDid: SimPol inferred belief networks from 2016 European Social Survey data across 23 countries and injected those structures into an agent-based model.
items.whatTheyFound: The simulated polarization patterns depended on belief rigidity and susceptibility to influence and reflected some geographic differences seen in empirical network structures.
items.whatItMeans: Empirical initialization makes simulations more defensible, but reproducing broad observed patterns does not establish prospective prediction or causal validity.

items.streamTitle: An FCM edge does not have to be one number
items.streamSummary: KA-FCM replaces each static Fuzzy Cognitive Map edge weight with an inspectable learned function, allowing the relationship between two variables to include thresholds, saturation, or even sign reversals. In computational tests it handled nonmonotonic relationships better than conventional FCMs while keeping the edge behavior visible. The approach is still a preprint, and fitting a flexible function from data does not solve confounding or causal identification, but it offers a useful route beyond constant-sign scalar edges.
items.questionAndWhy: Can Fuzzy Cognitive Map edges represent thresholds, saturation, and sign reversals instead of one scalar weight?
items.whatTheyDid: Salmeron proposed KA-FCM, replacing static edge weights with learnable univariate B-spline functions, and evaluated it on nonmonotonic, symbolic-regression, and chaotic time-series tasks.
items.whatTheyFound: The model represented relationships such as Yerkes–Dodson curves and outperformed conventional FCM baselines while keeping edge functions inspectable.
items.whatItMeans: Nonlinear edges can make FCMs more realistic without hiding relationships in a black box, but flexible curve fitting does not itself establish causality.

items.streamTitle: Moral licensing largely disappeared when nobody was watching
items.streamSummary: A preregistered meta-analysis of 115 experiments found that moral licensing—doing something good and then behaving less morally—was much stronger when people knew they were being observed. After adjustment for publication bias, the authors found moderate evidence for licensing under explicit observation but evidence against a meaningful effect when behavior was unobserved. The result suggests that reputation and audience presence may be central boundary conditions rather than background noise.
items.attribution: Rotella et al. — Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin
items.questionAndWhy: Does moral licensing persist when nobody is watching, or is the effect tied mainly to reputation and observation?
items.whatTheyDid: Rotella and colleagues conducted a preregistered moderator meta-analysis of 115 experiments involving 21,770 participants and adjusted estimates for publication bias.
items.whatTheyFound: Licensing was much larger under explicit observation and, after Bayesian bias adjustment, there was evidence against an effect when participants were unobserved.
items.whatItMeans: A phenomenon often framed as internal moral accounting may depend heavily on social observation. Context can determine whether an effect appears at all.

items.streamTitle: Moral language can help engagement—until it becomes too dense
items.streamSummary: An analysis of more than 1.6 million posts across Twitter, Reddit, and 8chan found a nonlinear relationship between moral language and engagement. Overall moral relevance was associated with more engagement, but concentrating too much moral content into a message was associated with less; engagement peaked at an intermediate density. The result challenges “more is better” assumptions in message optimization, although the study is observational and does not prove that experimentally increasing moral density would cause the same change.
items.attribution: Candia et al. — Nature Human Behaviour
items.questionAndWhy: Does moral language increase engagement indefinitely, or is there a saturation point?
items.whatTheyDid: Candia, Atari, Kteily and colleagues analyzed more than 1.6 million observations across 13 sociopolitical topics on Twitter, Reddit, and 8chan, separating overall moral loading from moral density.
items.whatTheyFound: Engagement rose with moral loading but, holding loading constant, fell when moral content became too dense; engagement peaked around a moral density of 0.30.
items.whatItMeans: Message features can have nonlinear dose-response relationships. The evidence is observational, so the shape should not be treated as an experimentally identified causal effect.

items.streamTitle: Germany’s drone attribution moved from accusation to a cost-imposition package
items.streamSummary: Germany’s attribution of the Leipzig/Halle drone incident was followed by concrete diplomatic measures and discussion of additional EU sanctions, while Russia denied responsibility. The development is useful because it shows attribution becoming an intervention package rather than remaining a statement about responsibility. The downstream effects are still open questions: imposed costs and allied endorsement do not themselves demonstrate deterrence or a change in future adversary behavior.
items.questionAndWhy: What happened after Germany publicly attributed the Leipzig/Halle drone incident, and did attribution translate into concrete cost-imposition?
items.whatTheyDid: Reuters documented Germany’s formal attribution, closure of Russia’s Bonn consulate, changes involving the Russian House, and EU discussion of further sanctions, alongside Russian denials.
items.whatTheyFound: Attribution moved from a responsibility claim into a diplomatic and sanctions response package with allied signaling.
items.whatItMeans: The next evaluative question is not whether a statement was issued but whether the package changes coalition behavior, domestic support, adversary expectations, or later hybrid activity.

items.streamTitle: LLMs can estimate average social norms well—but their errors look like a shared hivemind
items.streamSummary: A benchmark of 555 everyday U.S. scenarios found that several LLMs estimated population-average social norms more accurately than individual humans. But human errors were mostly independent, so pooling people improved estimates dramatically, while errors across LLMs were much more correlated and model ensembles added little. A hybrid human-plus-LLM estimate performed best. The result supports a bounded use for models as aggregate prior estimators and warns against treating multiple LLM personas as independent evidence about population diversity.
items.attribution: Eriksson et al. — Communications AI & Computing
items.questionAndWhy: How well can LLMs estimate aggregate U.S. social norms, and do multiple models provide independent perspectives like multiple humans?
items.whatTheyDid: Eriksson and colleagues benchmarked six LLMs and 320 humans on 555 scenarios with previously measured population norms and compared individual and ensemble errors.
items.whatTheyFound: Several LLMs beat average individuals, but their errors were highly correlated; aggregating humans improved sharply while aggregating LLMs added little. The best estimate combined humans and a model.
items.whatItMeans: LLMs can be useful population-prior estimators, but multiple models should not be treated as independent synthetic respondents when their errors share the same structure.

items.streamTitle: People do not automatically model their audience—but scaffolding can help
items.streamSummary: Three experiments found that people use a mix of sophisticated audience modeling and simpler heuristics when deciding what information to teach. Many participants persisted with a heuristic even after it stopped working, but a task that made it easier to infer what the learner knew substantially reduced that tendency. The finding suggests that poor audience analysis can result from cognitive demands, not just missing data, and that communication tools can improve performance by scaffolding the inference itself.
items.attribution: Harootonian et al. — Nature Human Behaviour
items.questionAndWhy: How do people choose information when teaching someone else, and can scaffolding help them reason about the learner instead of using simple heuristics?
items.whatTheyDid: Three behavioral experiments and computational models tested whether participants used Bayesian audience-state reasoning or simpler teaching heuristics.
items.whatTheyFound: People varied in strategy, often persisted with heuristics even when ineffective, and shifted toward more audience-sensitive reasoning when the learner-inference task was scaffolded.
items.whatItMeans: Audience modeling is cognitively demanding and can fail even when information is available. Making the inference step easier can change communication strategy.

items.streamTitle: Coalition causal discovery needs semantic and intervention governance
items.streamSummary: FLODO reframes causal discovery for settings where different agents see different variables, use different labels, and cannot simply pool all raw data. The protocol lets local agents exchange structural information while humans manage intervention strategy, semantic alignment, and disputed edges. It also treats simultaneous interventions as a source of contamination. The contribution is highly relevant to coalition and interagency analysis, although the peer-reviewed protocol remains an early framework rather than a broadly validated operational system.
items.questionAndWhy: How can multiple agents or organizations discover a causal graph when each sees only part of the system and cannot pool all raw data?
items.whatTheyDid: Gregorini and Meyer-Vitali proposed FLODO, a decentralized causal-discovery protocol in which agents exchange structural information and humans handle intervention strategy, semantic alignment, and unresolved edges.
items.whatTheyFound: The framework formalizes partial observability, semantic alignment, soft expert priors, and the risk that simultaneous interventions contaminate causal information.
items.whatItMeans: Causal discovery in coalition settings is also an organizational and semantic governance problem. The protocol is promising but still needs broader validation.

items.streamTitle: A dynamic FCM reconstructed famine-like conditions that static thresholds missed
items.streamSummary: A retrospective Fuzzy Cognitive Map integrated 21 factors and 74 weighted relationships to reconstruct the 2017 Ayod County famine crisis. The model generated a famine-like trajectory during months that later survey evidence supported, even though the area was never formally classified as famine by the static IPC process. The case illustrates how a dynamic systems model can integrate sparse evidence and feedback over time, while its largely expert-defined weights remain hypotheses rather than identified causal effects.
items.attribution: Matthew Day — Journal of Public Health Policy
items.questionAndWhy: Can a dynamic Fuzzy Cognitive Map reconstruct a crisis trajectory that static threshold classification misses?
items.whatTheyDid: Matthew Day built a 21-factor, 74-edge FCM of the 2017 Ayod County famine crisis using 242 evidence entries and four time-varying scenarios.
items.whatTheyFound: The model generated famine-like conditions during the period later supported by survey evidence even though the location was not formally classified as famine by the IPC.
items.whatItMeans: The value is dynamic integration and trajectory exploration in sparse-data settings, not proof that expert-weighted edges are causally identified.

items.streamTitle: ROK–U.S. I2E2 treats information effects as a coordination-system problem
items.streamSummary: The inaugural ROK–U.S. I2E2 tabletop exercise organized work around countering foreign disinformation, synchronizing cyber/space/electromagnetic responses, and aligning strategic communication across agencies and coalition partners.
