The important shift is upstream: the exercise treats coordination architecture, timing, attribution, and cross-domain consistency as part of the information-effect system. The official report documents process and institutionalization, not evidence that the resulting communications changed audience behavior.
items.questionAndWhy: How are the ROK–U.S. alliance and partners treating the information environment as a coordination problem rather than only a messaging problem?
items.whatTheyDid: The inaugural I2E2 tabletop exercise brought ROK, U.S., UN Command, Combined Forces Command, interagency, and coalition participants together around disinformation, cross-domain synchronization, and strategic communication.
items.whatTheyFound: The official report documented a coordination architecture and steady-state frameworks, but no public audience-behavior outcomes.
items.whatItMeans: Information effects can fail upstream through slow attribution, inconsistent actions, or poor organizational alignment. Coordination quality is a legitimate system variable even before message effectiveness is measured.

items.streamTitle: LLMs may be useful experiment forecasters even when they are not valid synthetic participants
items.streamSummary: A Nature validation study compared GPT-4 forecasts with hundreds of treatment effects from real preregistered experiments. The model captured the relative pattern of effects surprisingly well and performed similarly to pooled human forecasts, including on some studies unavailable before its training cutoff. It also systematically overestimated effect sizes. That makes the most defensible use case a screening layer—helping prioritize what to test—rather than treating simulated responses as empirical human evidence.
items.questionAndWhy: Can LLMs forecast average experimental treatment effects well enough to help decide which interventions deserve human testing?
items.whatTheyDid: Ashokkumar and colleagues compared GPT-4 forecasts against 70 preregistered nationally representative U.S. experiments with 469 effects and a second archive of 15 megastudies.
items.whatTheyFound: Model forecasts correlated strongly with real effects in the main archive and performed similarly to pooled human forecasts, but systematically overestimated effect sizes.
items.whatItMeans: LLMs may be useful as biased pre-experimental forecasters or prioritization tools, not as substitutes for human subjects or empirical effect estimates.

items.streamTitle: A truthful norm correction can move public and private behavior in different directions
items.streamSummary: A randomized experiment corrected participants’ beliefs about how many Americans support carbon taxation. The correction improved norm accuracy but did not increase average private climate donations; among people who had overestimated support, donations actually fell. At the same time, treated participants became more willing to take a publicly observable action. The study shows why norm interventions need baseline beliefs and behavior type: the same accurate information can have different—and sometimes opposite—effects across audiences and outcomes.
items.attribution: Galdikiene, Jaraite & Kajackaite — Journal of Economic Behavior & Organization
items.questionAndWhy: Does correcting a misperceived social norm change behavior in the same direction for everyone and across public and private actions?
items.whatTheyDid: A randomized experiment with 1,587 U.S. participants corrected beliefs about support for carbon taxation and measured an incentivized private donation plus willingness to attend a public policy discussion.
items.whatTheyFound: The correction reduced norm misperceptions, did not raise average private donations, reduced donations among prior overestimators, and increased willingness for the more publicly observable action.
items.whatItMeans: The same truthful correction can have different or opposite behavioral effects depending on prior beliefs and behavioral context. Average effects can hide meaningful boomerangs.

items.streamTitle: Physical proximity on the Senate floor measurably shifted real votes
items.streamSummary: An NBER natural experiment exploits U.S. Senate seating assignments to estimate peer influence on actual legislative votes. Senators seated near one another shifted each other’s voting by an estimated 11.9 percentage points, with effects concentrated within about 20 feet; computer-vision analysis of C-SPAN footage showed more face-to-face interaction among nearby members. The study highlights physical exposure opportunity as a real influence variable, while the observed interaction process is supporting mechanism evidence rather than a separately randomized mediator.
items.questionAndWhy: Does exogenously assigned physical proximity between U.S. senators change consequential legislative behavior?
items.whatTheyDid: Cohen and Li exploited Senate seating assignments and paired voting data with AI-assisted computer vision of C-SPAN interactions.
items.whatTheyFound: Closely seated peers shifted votes by an estimated 11.9 percentage points, with effects concentrated within roughly 19.6 feet and associated with more face-to-face interaction.
items.whatItMeans: Influence has an exposure geometry: physical proximity and repeated contact can shape high-stakes decisions. The natural-experiment estimate is stronger for the exposure effect than for the exact interpersonal mechanism.

items.streamTitle: Turning an algorithmic feed on changed attitudes and follow networks; turning it off did not simply reverse them
items.streamSummary: A seven-week randomized field experiment among active U.S. X users found that switching people from a chronological to an algorithmic feed increased engagement, shifted some political attitudes in a conservative direction, and led participants to follow more conservative activist accounts. Moving existing algorithmic-feed users to chronological feeds did not create an equal and opposite effect. The asymmetry matters because an exposure regime can alter the follow network that determines later exposure, creating path dependence beyond the immediate feed treatment.
items.questionAndWhy: Does switching between algorithmic and chronological feeds change political attitudes and behavior, and are the effects reversible?
items.whatTheyDid: A seven-week randomized field experiment independently assigned active U.S. X users to algorithmic or chronological feeds and measured engagement, attitudes, and following behavior.
items.whatTheyFound: Moving chronological users to the algorithmic feed increased engagement, shifted some attitudes in a conservative direction, and increased following of conservative activist accounts; switching algorithmic users off did not produce a symmetric reversal.
items.whatItMeans: Information environments can change the network that shapes later exposure, making effects path-dependent and potentially persistent after the original treatment changes.

items.streamTitle: Public attribution turns an intelligence judgment into a strategic intervention
items.streamSummary: German officials moved toward publicly blaming Russia for an attempted explosive-drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport, according to Reuters, while signaling possible consequences. The important analytical point is not only who is blamed: public attribution itself can shape allied cohesion, public threat perception, support for countermeasures, and adversary expectations. Because the underlying intelligence is not fully public and Moscow denied responsibility, the attribution claim should remain distinct from independently established ground truth.
items.questionAndWhy: How does public attribution of a suspected hybrid attack become a strategic action rather than merely an intelligence conclusion?
items.whatTheyDid: Reuters reported that German officials were preparing to attribute an attempted explosive-drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport to Russia and were considering consequences.
items.whatTheyFound: The reporting showed attribution moving into public diplomacy and possible sanctions, while the underlying intelligence basis remained partly non-public.
items.whatItMeans: Attribution can shape allied consensus, threat perception, legitimacy for countermeasures, and adversary expectations. A government attribution is not the same thing as independent proof.

items.streamTitle: Defensive states can change how threat and reward are weighed
items.streamSummary: A high-precision neuroscience study found that threat-related cardiac slowing was associated with stronger weighting of both threat and reward during approach–avoidance decisions. Neural value signals also predicted choices before the overt response. The result complicates the simple idea that stronger defensive reactions always mean more avoidance: physiological state may change how competing information is integrated. The evidence is strong for the laboratory task but should not be generalized directly to real-world crisis or deterrence decisions.
items.questionAndWhy: Can defensive physiological states change how people weigh threat and reward during decisions?
items.whatTheyDid: Klaassen and colleagues used high-precision MEG and cardiac measures during an approach–avoidance task that required participants to trade reward against danger.
items.whatTheyFound: Threat-related cardiac deceleration was associated with stronger weighting of both threat and reward information, and neural value signals predicted later choices.
items.whatItMeans: Defensive states may change information weighting rather than simply pushing people toward avoidance. The evidence is laboratory-based and does not establish real-world crisis or deterrence behavior.

items.streamTitle: Behavioral theory needs a formalization layer before it becomes an agent rule
items.streamSummary: MOZAIC provides a systematic way to translate verbal social-science theories into mathematical decision rules for agent-based models. The authors demonstrate the method with rational choice, bounded rationality, habit, prospect theory, and descriptive norms, producing reusable mathematical building blocks. The contribution addresses a common problem: two simulations can cite the same theory but implement it very differently. Formalization makes those choices inspectable, though it does not prove that a particular mathematical function is correct for a target population.
items.questionAndWhy: How can verbal behavioral theories be translated into explicit mathematical decision rules for agent-based models?
items.whatTheyDid: The MOZAIC framework formalized a four-step process and demonstrated it across rational choice, bounded rationality, habit, prospect theory, and descriptive norms.
items.whatTheyFound: It produced reusable mathematical building blocks intended to make theory implementations more transparent and comparable.
items.whatItMeans: Naming a theory in a simulation is not enough; modelers need to specify how constructs become states, equations, thresholds, and action probabilities. Formalization improves transparency but does not validate the chosen function empirically.

items.streamTitle: Influence simulation needs networks and narrative dynamics—not just personas
items.streamSummary: The LAND/GhostField demonstration simulated more than 314,000 cyber-social agents and human actors exchanging over half a million messages across a month-long synthetic scenario. Its central design choice is important: influence emerges from the interaction of network structure, repeated exposure, and evolving discourse rather than from persona traits alone. The scale and architecture are notable, but the scenario remains synthetic; convincing emergent agent behavior is not evidence that real populations would behave the same way.
items.questionAndWhy: Can large LLM-agent simulations represent influence as an emergent interaction between network structure and evolving narratives?
items.whatTheyDid: Ng and Carley introduced LAND/GhostField and simulated more than 314,000 cyber-social agents and human actors exchanging over 529,000 messages across 30 simulated days.
items.whatTheyFound: Coordination and influence emerged recursively from interactions between network topology and narrative exchange in the synthetic scenario.
items.whatItMeans: The architecture moves beyond isolated personas toward a networked social system, but its emergent behavior has not been validated as predictive of real humans.

items.streamTitle: LLM social simulation needs a protocol and an audit trail
items.streamSummary: MASS turns LLM-agent role-play into a more explicit research protocol by specifying roles, information boundaries, round schedules, scenario rules, structured outputs, logs, model versions, and validation targets. The framework was demonstrated across three real-world-inspired cases and is designed to make simulations easier to audit and reproduce. Its authors appropriately frame it as mechanism rehearsal and research-design preparation rather than a replacement for experiments or causal inference.
items.questionAndWhy: How can LLM-agent social simulations be made auditable and reproducible instead of being hidden prompt-driven role-play?
items.whatTheyDid: Hu and Shen proposed MASS, a protocol that makes role settings, round schedules, information boundaries, rules, structured outputs, logs, model versions, validation targets, and replication manifests explicit.
items.whatTheyFound: The protocol was demonstrated across three real-world-inspired cases and exposed common failure modes such as role drift, rule violations, future leakage, and replication difficulty.
items.whatItMeans: Prompting and simulation setup should be treated as research-design parameters. MASS is useful for mechanism rehearsal and design preparation, not a substitute for causal evidence.

items.streamTitle: Community Notes sharply reduced later reposting—but often arrived after the viral phase
items.streamSummary: A large quasi-experimental study of 237,180 fact-checked cascades on X estimated that Community Notes reduced subsequent reposting by 61.2% after display and substantially increased author deletion. The catch was timing: notes often appeared only after a post had already experienced its fastest growth. The study therefore separates treatment efficacy from system effectiveness. A correction can work once delivered and still have limited total impact if it arrives too late.
items.questionAndWhy: How much does displaying a Community Note reduce the subsequent spread of a misleading post, and how much does timing limit the overall effect?
items.whatTheyDid: A large Difference-in-Differences study analyzed 237,180 fact-checked cascades on X containing more than 431 million reposts.
items.whatTheyFound: After a note appeared, subsequent reposting fell by an estimated 61.2% and author deletion increased, but notes frequently arrived after the earliest viral phase.
items.whatItMeans: An intervention can be effective after delivery while the system remains limited by latency. Operational effectiveness depends on effect size, coverage, timing, and uptake.

items.streamTitle: A major influencer measurably shifted high-stakes university-major choices
items.streamSummary: A natural experiment using more than 3.3 million Chinese admissions observations linked a prominent influencer’s public advice to changes in real university-major choices. A negative signal about Journalism and Communication was followed by substantially worse admission ranks, especially at elite universities, while an endorsed field saw smaller positive effects. The design includes event-study and placebo checks, making this unusually strong evidence on consequential behavior, though the specific psychological mechanism and transfer to other contexts remain less certain.
items.questionAndWhy: Can a prominent social-media influencer measurably change consequential education choices rather than just online engagement?
items.whatTheyDid: Researchers used more than 3.3 million Chinese university-admissions observations in a Difference-in-Differences natural experiment around a viral influencer’s recommendations.
items.whatTheyFound: A negative signal about Journalism and Communication was associated with a 13.1% worsening in admission rank overall and 24.7% at elite universities, with smaller positive effects for an endorsed field.
items.whatItMeans: The study connects a prominent source and message valence to real high-stakes behavior at large scale, although the exact psychological mechanism is less directly identified and the admissions context is distinctive.

items.streamTitle: Peer praise changed behavior without increasing the empathy it was designed to activate
items.streamSummary: A large Registered Report tested peer praise as a way to motivate empathy toward racial outgroups. Average empathy and willingness to engage empathically did not increase, yet participants became more likely to write letters advocating racial equality. That mismatch is the important result: an intervention can affect behavior even when the mechanism it was designed around does not move. The study is a strong reminder not to infer how an intervention worked from its label or intent.
items.questionAndWhy: Can peer praise motivate empathy and produce more inclusive political behavior?
items.whatTheyDid: A large Registered Report tested a peer-praise intervention among more than 9,000 U.S. respondents across a main and co-partisan experiment.
items.whatTheyFound: The intervention did not increase average empathy or willingness to empathize, but it did increase one inclusive political behavior: writing letters advocating racial equality.
items.whatItMeans: An intervention can move behavior without moving its intended mediator. Mechanism claims should be revised when the proposed pathway does not respond.

items.streamTitle: Reducing polarization did not reduce false-news sharing—but an accuracy prompt helped
items.streamSummary: A randomized experiment separately changed feelings toward the opposing political party and made accuracy salient before a news-sharing task. Improving out-party affect did not measurably improve participants’ ability to distinguish true from false stories when deciding what to share, while the accuracy prompt did. The finding challenges the assumption that reducing affective polarization will automatically reduce misinformation sharing. The outcome was sharing intention in an experimental setting, not observed platform behavior.
items.questionAndWhy: Does reducing hostility toward the opposing political party reduce false-news sharing?
items.whatTheyDid: A randomized 2×2 experiment independently manipulated out-party affect and accuracy salience before a news-sharing task.
items.whatTheyFound: Improving feelings toward the opposing party did not measurably improve truth discernment, while an accuracy prompt did.
items.whatItMeans: A socially important correlate can still be the wrong intervention target for a specific behavior. Accuracy salience was more useful for sharing discernment in this experiment.

items.streamTitle: FCMs can search backward from an objective to candidate changes
items.streamSummary: CF-BP adds an inverse capability to Fuzzy Cognitive Maps: rather than only asking what follows from a change, it searches for minimal modeled input changes that would move a target outcome. The peer-reviewed method uses analytical gradients and performed well against several counterfactual baselines. That can be valuable for decision support, but “causally consistent” here means consistent with the relationships encoded in the FCM; it does not prove those relationships are causally correct in the real world.
items.attribution: Tyrovolas, Nápoles & Stylios — IEEE Transactions on Systems, Man, and Cybernetics
items.questionAndWhy: Can an FCM search backward from a desired outcome to identify minimal modeled state changes that would reach it?
items.whatTheyDid: Tyrovolas, Nápoles, and Stylios introduced CF-BP, which uses analytical gradients through quasi-nonlinear FCMs to generate counterfactual state changes.
items.whatTheyFound: The method outperformed several model-agnostic counterfactual techniques on reported quality and robustness measures while respecting dependencies encoded in the FCM.
items.whatItMeans: Counterfactual search can make an FCM useful for intervention discovery, but the recommendations are only as causally credible as the model they operate on.

items.streamTitle: NATO StratCom is bringing synthetic audiences into live training
items.streamSummary: SYNESIS 2026 will combine AI-enabled agents, real-time simulation, and Audience Behaviour Modelling in a NATO StratCom COE live exercise focused on hostile information influence and hybrid threats. The development matters because synthetic audiences are moving into operationally relevant training rather than remaining academic demos. What is not yet public is equally important: there is no demonstrated evidence that the simulated audience responses predict how real people would respond.
items.questionAndWhy: How is NATO StratCom bringing AI-enabled audience simulation into an operational training environment?
items.whatTheyDid: NATO StratCom COE described SYNESIS 2026 as an AI-enabled live exercise combining agent systems, real-time simulation, and Audience Behaviour Modelling.
items.whatTheyFound: The program places synthetic audience response inside practitioner training for hostile information influence and hybrid-threat scenarios.
items.whatItMeans: Audience simulation is moving from academic demonstrations into operational training, increasing the importance of validating whether simulated responses meaningfully resemble real audience behavior.

items.streamTitle: Taiwan’s election warning turns “cognitive warfare” into observable conduct categories
items.streamSummary: Taiwan’s governing DPP China Affairs Department published a set of concrete election-interference behaviors it says can trigger legal consequences, including directed travel, benefits for political support, foreign-funded polling or propaganda, intermediaries, and intelligence-related activity. The useful analytical move is from an umbrella label to observable conduct and evidence artifacts. Because the warning comes from a political actor with direct electoral interests, it should be read as a defensive threat model rather than proof of how prevalent or effective each tactic is.
items.attribution: Taipei Times / DPP China Affairs Department
items.questionAndWhy: How is Taiwan translating the broad label “cognitive warfare” into specific election-interference behaviors and evidence artifacts?
items.whatTheyDid: Taiwan’s governing DPP China Affairs Department publicly listed conduct categories such as directed travel, inducements, fake polling, commissioned propaganda, intermediaries, and organizational activity, and urged preservation of concrete records.
items.whatTheyFound: The warning operationalized an umbrella threat concept into observable behaviors, coordination indicators, funding/tasking clues, and evidentiary artifacts, while not proving the prevalence or effectiveness of each tactic.
items.whatItMeans: Threat analysis becomes more useful when sponsorship, intermediaries, content, benefits, coordination, and audience response are represented separately. The partisan source context warrants caution.

items.streamTitle: Synthetic respondents can sound diverse while being statistically repetitive
items.streamSummary: A psychometric validation study found that GPT-generated survey respondents used less of the response range, repeated patterns more often, and occupied a narrower multivariate space than a human reference sample. More than 5% of synthetic profiles gave the same response across all 42 items, compared with 0.7% of human profiles, even though the model’s free-text explanations sounded varied. The finding is model- and instrument-specific, but it shows why fluent prose is a poor substitute for distributional validation.
items.questionAndWhy: Can synthetic respondents sound diverse while remaining statistically narrow compared with real human response patterns?
items.whatTheyDid: Mazzullo and Bulut compared GPT-3.5-Turbo questionnaire responses with a large human reference dataset, examining response ranges, repetition, within-profile variability, and multivariate distributional coverage.
items.whatTheyFound: Synthetic responses used less of the scale, repeated more, occupied a narrower multivariate region, and produced far more invariant profiles even while free-text explanations remained lexically diverse.
items.whatItMeans: Linguistic variety can hide psychometric collapse. Synthetic-audience validation needs distributional and within-person checks, not judgments that the prose “sounds human.”

items.streamTitle: Use the LLM to operate the model—not to be the model
items.streamSummary: A crowd-management digital-twin prototype pairs a conversational Gemini interface with an explicit agent-based simulation engine. The simulator, not the LLM, governs movement, queues, occupancy, balking, and evacuation, while natural language is used to configure scenarios and inspect results. The architecture is attractive because it keeps behavioral rules auditable. The prototype reached technical scale in synthetic scenarios, but it has not yet demonstrated real-time calibration or predictive validity against actual crowd events.
items.questionAndWhy: Can an LLM provide a natural-language interface to a digital twin while leaving the actual behavioral dynamics in an explicit simulation engine?
items.whatTheyDid: A crowd-management prototype combined an agent-based/discrete-time simulator, API orchestration, and a Gemini 2.5 Flash interface for configuring and querying scenarios.
items.whatTheyFound: The explicit simulator—not the LLM—controlled arrivals, movement, queues, occupancy, and evacuation and scaled to 60,000 simulated attendees in tests, but real-time empirical synchronization was not yet demonstrated.
items.whatItMeans: This architecture separates interface/orchestration from behavioral rules, improving auditability. The LLM can operate and explain a model without silently becoming the model.

items.streamTitle: Acknowledgment can create common ground without requiring agreement
items.streamSummary: In a preregistered randomized study of 558 U.S. adults, messages that affirmed either an opposing viewpoint’s arguments or its intentions improved perceived perspective-taking, fairness, similarity, common ground, and anticipated relationship quality. The finding suggests that acknowledgment can improve the relational conditions for disagreement without requiring agreement. These are immediate relational outcomes, however, not evidence of durable persuasion or long-term behavior change.
items.questionAndWhy: Can acknowledging the arguments or intentions behind an opposing position create relational common ground without requiring agreement?
items.whatTheyDid: A preregistered randomized experiment with 558 U.S. adults tested messages that affirmed either the opposing side’s arguments or its intentions.
items.whatTheyFound: Both forms improved perceived perspective-taking, fairness, similarity, common ground, and anticipated relationship quality; argument acknowledgment was estimated to be stronger on several outcomes.
items.whatItMeans: Acknowledgment can improve the relational conditions for disagreement, but the study did not establish durable persuasion or real-world behavior change.

items.streamTitle: Calling symptoms “normal” can unintentionally signal that treatment is unnecessary
items.streamSummary: Across 14 studies involving 9,371 participants, reassurance that described symptoms as “normal” reduced reported willingness to seek treatment. The effect was not explained only by reduced anxiety: participants inferred an implicit treatment norm, as though “normal” also meant “you do not need to act.” The work is a strong example of unintended pragmatic inference and shows why communicators should distinguish prevalence from recommended action. The studies were largely online, so real clinical behavior still needs field validation.
items.questionAndWhy: Can reassuring people that symptoms are “normal” unintentionally communicate that treatment is unnecessary?
items.whatTheyDid: Across 14 studies with 9,371 participants, researchers tested symptom-normalization messages, treatment intentions, inferred norms, and alternative wording that preserved reassurance while clarifying treatment intent.
items.whatTheyFound: Describing symptoms as normal reduced inclination to pursue treatment largely because people inferred an implicit norm that treatment was not warranted, not simply because anxiety fell.
items.whatItMeans: Literal content is not the whole message. Descriptive normality can leak into an injunctive recommendation, creating the opposite action signal from what the communicator intended.

items.streamTitle: Social influence becomes clearer when you specify who, where, how, and which behavior
items.streamSummary: A Nature Climate Change perspective proposes a four-part way to unpack social influence: who is influencing, where influence is directed, how influence occurs, and which behavior is targeted. The value is less a new psychological effect than a disciplined schema for comparing interventions and evidence. It prevents “influence” from being used simultaneously as actor, method, mechanism, and outcome. The framework comes from climate-action research, so specific interaction effects still need testing in other settings.
items.attribution: Hampton, Latter & Whitmarsh — Nature Climate Change
items.questionAndWhy: Can the broad concept of social influence be decomposed into a compact set of variables that make studies and interventions easier to compare?
items.whatTheyDid: Hampton, Latter, and Whitmarsh synthesized climate communication and behavioral science into four interacting dimensions: who influences, where influence is directed, how it occurs, and which behavior is targeted.
items.whatTheyFound: The review shows that source, audience, mechanism, target behavior, and context interact and that many real-world combinations remain under-tested.
items.whatItMeans: The main contribution is structural rather than a new effect: “influence” should be unpacked before analysts compare methods or claim outcomes.

items.streamTitle: Double Machine Learning offers a path from expert FCM edges to empirical estimates
items.streamSummary: A causal-mapping preprint treats each stakeholder-defined FCM edge as a treatment–outcome hypothesis and estimates selected edge strengths from longitudinal data with Double Machine Learning. Synthetic tests and a real socio-environmental application show how expert topology and data-driven estimation can coexist. The method is promising because it differs from simply optimizing weights for predictive fit, but it remains a preprint and still depends on confounding, measurement, temporal-ordering, and graph-validity assumptions.
items.questionAndWhy: Can expert-defined FCM relationships be treated as causal hypotheses whose weights are estimated from longitudinal data rather than assigned subjectively?
items.whatTheyDid: Neri-Barranco and colleagues proposed causal inference cognitive mapping, using Double Machine Learning with temporal lags and forward-chaining cross-fitting to estimate selected stakeholder-defined FCM edges.
items.whatTheyFound: Synthetic tests showed low bias and high sign accuracy, and the method was applied to a multidecadal stakeholder map of the Middle Rio Grande.
items.whatItMeans: The promising hybrid is governance by theory/SMEs plus empirical estimation where identification is defensible. DML still cannot solve unmeasured confounding or incorrect graph structure.

items.streamTitle: NATO is institutionalizing cognitive resilience—but measurement still lags
items.streamSummary: NATO Defense College’s 2026 Conference of Commandants brought together 108 participants from 67 defense institutions around cognitive warfare and resilience. The official synthesis shows the concept moving into professional education, defense planning, and capability development, with emphasis on biases, emotion, trust, and decision-making. What remains unclear is effectiveness: the event documents institutional adoption, not whether particular curricula measurably improve decisions under manipulation or uncertainty. The next step is turning “resilience” into specific trainable and testable capabilities.
items.questionAndWhy: How is NATO moving cognitive resilience from a concept into professional military education, and what would it take to measure it?
items.whatTheyDid: NATO Defense College convened 108 participants from 67 defense institutions around “The Mind as a Battlespace,” linking cognitive warfare to education, planning, capability development, biases, emotion, trust, and decision-making.
items.whatTheyFound: The official synthesis shows institutional adoption of cognitive-resilience training objectives but does not provide evidence that specific curricula improve operational decision performance.
items.whatItMeans: The emerging gap is measurement: cognitive resilience needs explicit, testable capabilities such as source verification, uncertainty management, trust calibration, manipulation resistance, and decision quality.

items.streamTitle: Changing the feed changed exposure and norm perception—but not users’ own engagement behavior
items.streamSummary: An eight-week randomized feed experiment around the 2024 U.S. election found that engagement-based ranking increased exposure to moralized, intergroup, emotional, and toxic political content and reduced the accuracy of users’ perceptions of social norms. A diversified feed improved norm accuracy while preserving enjoyment. Yet the ranking intervention did not significantly change users’ own engagement behavior. The result is a useful reminder that exposure, social perception, and behavior can move independently even inside the same causal experiment.
items.questionAndWhy: Does changing social-media feed ranking alter what users see, what they think others believe, and what they themselves do?
items.whatTheyDid: A Registered Report randomly assigned 2,000 participants to custom feed-ranking algorithms for eight weeks around the 2024 U.S. presidential election.
items.whatTheyFound: Engagement-based ranking increased exposure to intergroup, moralized, emotional, and toxic content and reduced norm accuracy; a diversified feed improved norm accuracy, but users’ own engagement behavior did not significantly change.
items.whatItMeans: Exposure, perception, and behavior are distinct outcome levels. A causal effect upstream does not imply a behavioral effect downstream.

items.streamTitle: Behavioral experiments can provide the thresholds used in diffusion models
items.streamSummary: A Nature Human Behaviour study estimated individual adoption thresholds from behavioral choice experiments and then used those thresholds inside network-diffusion simulations. The simulations showed that strategies based only on network position can be suboptimal when people differ in how much social exposure they need before adopting. The contribution is methodological: it links measured micro-level behavior to agent parameters instead of inventing universal thresholds. How well the approach transfers depends on the behavior, population, and network being modeled.
items.attribution: Tănase, Algesheimer & Mariani — Nature Human Behaviour
items.questionAndWhy: Can behavioral experiments estimate individual adoption thresholds that then improve network-diffusion simulations?
items.whatTheyDid: Tănase, Algesheimer, and Mariani estimated person-level adoption thresholds in choice experiments and inserted those empirically estimated thresholds into complex-contagion simulations.
items.whatTheyFound: Seeding strategies that ignored heterogeneous thresholds could be suboptimal; measured susceptibility and network position jointly shaped diffusion outcomes in the simulations.
items.whatItMeans: This closes a common modeling gap: agent thresholds can come from observed choices rather than arbitrary assumptions. Transfer to other behaviors still requires calibration.

items.streamTitle: News trust fell while use of the trusted source increased
items.streamSummary: A field experiment with readers of Süddeutsche Zeitung warned about the difficulty of distinguishing real from AI-generated images. Concern about misinformation rose and reported trust in news fell, including trust in the newspaper itself. Yet readers visited the outlet more afterward and subscriber retention was higher five months later. The result shows why survey attitudes and revealed behavior should be measured separately: a warning can make the information environment feel less trustworthy while increasing the relative value of a source people already rely on.
items.questionAndWhy: Can warning people about generative-AI misinformation reduce trust in news while still increasing their use of a trusted news outlet?
items.whatTheyDid: A preregistered field experiment with readers of Süddeutsche Zeitung randomly emphasized the difficulty of distinguishing real from AI-generated images and tracked surveys, browsing, and five-month subscriber retention.
items.whatTheyFound: The warning increased misinformation concern and reduced reported trust in news, including the outlet itself, while increasing immediate site visits and improving subscriber retention months later.
items.whatItMeans: Attitudes and revealed behavior can point in different directions. When trace data exist, a proximal trust measure should not substitute for the operational outcome.

items.streamTitle: A causal digital twin asks who benefits from the intervention—not just who is at risk
items.streamSummary: DINIRS combines patient-state modeling with doubly robust causal estimation to predict how different patients might respond to alternative respiratory-support strategies. External validation strengthened the proof of concept, but the individual counterfactual effects remain observational estimates and the authors call for prospective testing. The broader lesson is useful beyond medicine: decision support should distinguish predicting an outcome from estimating how an intervention changes that outcome for different people.
items.questionAndWhy: Can a digital-twin model estimate who benefits from one intervention versus another rather than simply predicting who is at risk?
items.whatTheyDid: DINIRS used baseline clinical variables, a transformer representation, and cross-fitted doubly robust estimation to estimate individualized effects of respiratory-support choices, then externally checked patterns in another ICU dataset.
items.whatTheyFound: The model estimated heterogeneous treatment benefits and a policy-level improvement in ventilator-free days, while the authors called for prospective validation before clinical use.
items.whatItMeans: The transferable idea is prediction versus intervention: a useful decision twin should estimate treatment-response differences under explicit identification assumptions, not merely forecast outcomes.

items.streamTitle: A realistic synthetic population is not automatically a valid synthetic human
items.streamSummary: Animarium released a deterministic pipeline that builds more than 1.8 million synthetic people and 887,000 households for 11 Italian municipalities from public demographic and survey data. The project tracks provenance and distinguishes empirically constrained attributes from generated biographies, while explicitly declining to claim behavioral validity. That separation is valuable for synthetic-audience work: a population can be statistically plausible and reproducible without proving that generated agents will respond like real people.
items.questionAndWhy: Can a synthetic population be built reproducibly from public data without pretending that demographic realism proves behavioral realism?
items.whatTheyDid: Animarium constructed 1.8 million synthetic individuals in 11 Italian municipalities from aggregate and survey data, with household constraints, spatial placement, provenance tracking, and deterministic generation.
items.whatTheyFound: The pipeline achieved reproducible population synthesis and explicitly labeled biographies and personas as derived artifacts while leaving behavioral validation out of scope.
items.whatItMeans: This is a useful architectural boundary: empirical population construction, persona rendering, and behavioral simulation should be validated separately. Detailed synthetic people are not automatically valid synthetic humans.

items.streamTitle: AI permission policies reduced prompts but made overreach protection worse
items.streamSummary: In a controlled study, reusable user-written permission rules reduced how often an AI agent had to ask for approval, but they also blocked less overreach than per-action human approval or automated review. Most overreach that still occurred under the policy condition followed an explicit human approval in context. The result highlights a behavioral governance problem: stated standing preferences are not always durable commitments when convenience, urgency, or trust enters the moment of action.
items.questionAndWhy: Do reusable user-written permission rules reduce AI-agent overreach as well as asking people to approve each consequential action?
items.whatTheyDid: A human-subjects study compared per-action approval, automated review, and reusable allow/ask/never policies across a simulated day containing normal and overreach actions.
items.whatTheyFound: User-authored policies reduced prompts but blocked substantially less overreach, and most overreach that occurred under the policy condition followed an explicit human approval at runtime.
items.whatItMeans: The failure surface was behavioral as well as technical: standing preferences can weaken when users face concrete, convenient requests. Human-in-the-loop control can become habitual click-through.

items.streamTitle: True content can still create a false inference
items.streamSummary: RCMN reframes misleadingness as a relationship between a message, its evidence, and the interpretation a reader is likely to draw. Its dataset includes unsupported inference, exaggeration, omission, arousal, and intent rather than treating misinformation as fabrication alone. Foundation models often recovered likely interpretations more easily than the actual misleading mechanism. The framework is still a preprint, but it offers a useful analytical reminder: factual accuracy and audience interpretation are not the same variable.
items.questionAndWhy: Can misleadingness be represented as the interpretation a message produces rather than a simple true-or-false label?
items.whatTheyDid: RCMN proposed five dimensions—misleading mechanism, likely reader interpretation, evidence-warranted interpretation, emotional arousal, and intent—and benchmarked foundation models on the resulting dataset.
items.whatTheyFound: The framework captured misleadingness caused by unsupported inference, exaggeration, and omission as well as fabrication; likely interpretation was often easier to recover than the mechanism that produced it.
items.whatItMeans: Technically true content can still predictably create evidence-inconsistent interpretations. Influence analysis should therefore separate factuality, framing mechanism, audience inference, and downstream behavior.

items.streamTitle: Cleaning a survey can make the sample more biased
items.streamSummary: Pew tested several ways to remove bogus respondents from an online opt-in survey of more than 11,000 U.S. adults. Trap questions and prescreening improved multiple quality indicators, but voter-file matching sometimes removed legitimate people who were harder to identify while retaining some bogus respondents, and all screening approaches shifted substantive estimates. The practical lesson is that “cleaning” data is not neutral: screening can create selection bias that matters for audience analysis and model calibration.
items.questionAndWhy: Can methods used to remove bogus online-survey respondents create their own selection bias?
items.whatTheyDid: Pew compared impossible-behavior trap questions, prescreening, and voter-file matching in an opt-in survey of more than 11,000 U.S. adults and examined both quality metrics and substantive estimates.
items.whatTheyFound: Trap questions and prescreening improved several quality indicators, but voter-file matching could remove legitimate respondents and worsen some estimates; every screening regime changed substantive turnout and vote-choice results.
items.whatItMeans: Data cleaning is itself an intervention on the sample. A validation method can improve identity confidence while making the target population less representative.

items.streamTitle: Sensors are not states—and states are not mission effects
items.streamSummary: An ARES 2026 cyber-defense model separates three layers that are often collapsed: observed telemetry, inferred adversary/system state, and mission-level risk. Bayesian updates feed a higher-level decision model that weighs residual risk against action cost, with robustness checks under noisy telemetry. The specific cyber model is domain-bound, but the architecture is broadly useful for decision support because it makes uncertainty and abstraction explicit instead of treating an indicator as the underlying condition.
items.questionAndWhy: How can noisy observations be translated into uncertain beliefs about system state and then into mission-level decisions without collapsing those layers?
items.whatTheyDid: An ARES 2026 model combined an attack graph, Bayesian event inference, and higher-level mission-risk states in an executable cyber-defense simulation.
items.whatTheyFound: Telemetry updated beliefs about adversary progression, those beliefs were abstracted into mission states, and decision rules compared residual risk with action cost under robustness tests.
items.whatItMeans: The architecture is a useful pattern for analytical systems: observations are not states, states are not mission effects, and each transformation should preserve uncertainty.

items.streamTitle: Visible messages can miss the state changes happening inside an influence network
items.streamSummary: A controlled LLM-agent benchmark found that direct exposure reliably shifted later probed stances, peer relays carried smaller effects, and the agents’ visible messages did not always reveal the stance changes measured internally. The agents are not validated substitutes for humans, so this is not evidence of human persuasion dynamics. Its value is methodological: influence measurement should preserve who saw what, through whom, what state changed, and what action followed instead of treating content volume as the effect.
items.questionAndWhy: How do persuasion effects propagate through LLM-agent networks, and can visible messages miss changes in underlying model state?
items.whatTheyDid: Researchers ran controlled multi-agent persuasion experiments across several LLM backbones, network topologies, topics, and competing persuaders while tracking exposure, stance probes, relays, and actions.
items.whatTheyFound: Direct exposure predicted later stance movement, peer relays carried smaller effects, and probed stance changes sometimes diverged from what agents said or did in surface text.
items.whatItMeans: The simulation is not evidence about human persuasion, but it highlights a measurement lesson: messages, latent state, action, network position, and exposure path should be tracked separately.

items.streamTitle: AI-generated election prebunks moved from experiment to a reusable tool
items.streamSummary: A preregistered panel experiment with 4,293 U.S. voters found that LLM-generated prebunking articles reduced belief in election rumors and modestly protected confidence in election administration, with smaller effects still visible a week later. Once researchers had refined the underlying template, fully AI-generated messages performed comparably to versions receiving per-rumor human feedback. The work shows how validated behavioral design can be front-loaded before automation, although the outcomes were self-reported beliefs rather than field behavior.
items.questionAndWhy: Can AI-generated prebunking messages reduce election-rumor belief at scale without requiring bespoke human writing for every rumor?
items.whatTheyDid: A preregistered two-wave experiment with 4,293 registered U.S. voters tested LLM-generated election prebunks, including versions with and without per-rumor human feedback, and later released a practitioner tool.
items.whatTheyFound: The prebunks reduced rumor belief, modestly protected confidence in election administration, showed no partisan backlash in the study, and retained attenuated effects after one week. Once the template was refined, fully AI-written versions were not less effective than human-reviewed variants.
items.whatItMeans: The key design pattern is to front-load expert constraints into a validated template and use generation for adaptation. The evidence concerns measured beliefs and confidence, not field behavior.
